q.q: What is misinformation?
o: False information shared by someone who believes it

q.q: What is disinformation?
o: False information shared on purpose to deceive

q.q: What is malinformation?
o: True information shared to cause harm
q.why: It's real information used to hurt.

q.q: What is the key difference between misinformation and disinformation?
o: The intent of the person sharing it

q.q: A fake story is made up to earn advert money. This is...
Your uncle shares a fake cure believing it works. He is spreading...
q.why: He believes it, so it's misinformation.

q.q: How does disinformation often become misinformation?
o: It turns into a true story
People share it believing it's true

q.q: Which is a common motive for creating disinformation?
Satire becomes misinformation when...
o: people share it believing it's real

q.q: Why does false health information matter?
o: It can lead people to make dangerous choices

q.q: Where does the word "deepfake" come from?
q.why: Deep learning is a type of AI.

q.q: What is a deepfake?
o: AI-made media of a real person doing or saying something they didn't

q.q: Which type of deepfake puts one person's face onto another's body?
A lip-sync deepfake...
o: changes the mouth in a real video to match new words

q.q: Roughly how much audio can some tools need to clone a voice?
q.why: Modern tools need very little audio.

q.q: Why are public figures common deepfake targets?
o: Their faces are easier to draw
AI can only copy famous people
Lots of video and audio of them is online to train AI

q.q: What did early deepfakes often get wrong?
q.why: Glitches were common in early fakes.

q.q: Why is it harder to spot deepfakes by eye today?
o: AI tools have improved and remove obvious glitches

q.q: Which is a harmful use of voice cloning?
o: A scam call pretending to be a family member
An audiobook read in an approved voice
Dubbing a film with the actor's permission
Helping someone who lost their voice

q.q: Is making a deepfake of a classmate "as a joke" OK?
o: No: it's done without consent and can be bullying
Yes, if you delete it later
Yes, if only friends see it
q.why: Consent matters; it can cause real harm.

q.q: What is a reverse image search?
o: Searching the web with a picture to find where it appears
q.why: It finds other copies of an image.

q.q: Which tool can you use for a reverse image search?
A reverse image search shows a "new" photo first appeared in 2016. What does this suggest?
o: It's an old photo being reshared as new

q.q: What is metadata?
o: Hidden information stored with a file

q.q: Which could photo metadata include?
o: The date it was taken and the device used
q.why: EXIF data stores details like date and device.

q.q: Why might metadata be missing from an image online?
o: Many social media sites remove it on upload

q.q: What is provenance?
o: The history of where something came from

q.q: What are content credentials?
o: A secure record of how a file was made and edited
A login for a news site

q.q: Which organisation created the content credentials standard?
q.why: C2PA is a group of tech, camera and media companies.

q.q: Why is it risky for metadata to stay on photos you share?
q.why: GPS data can show where you were.

q.q: What is the best approach to checking a viral photo?
o: Ask the person who posted it if it's real
Combine clues: source, reverse search, metadata and credentials

q.q: What is lateral reading?
o: Checking a source by seeing what other trusted sources say about it

q.q: What does SIFT stand for?
o: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace to the original
q.why: SIFT is a four-step checking routine.

q.q: Why is "Stop" the first SIFT step?
o: Disinformation aims to make you react before thinking

q.q: "Investigate the source" means...
o: finding out who made it and why

q.q: "Find better coverage" means...
o: checking whether trusted outlets report the claim

q.q: "Trace claims to the original" means...
o: finding where a quote or picture really came from

q.q: Which is the strongest sign a source may be reliable?
o: It has named experts, cites evidence and corrects mistakes

q.q: Which is a warning sign about a website?
o: Anonymous authors and a history of clickbait
q.why: Anonymity and clickbait are red flags.

q.q: Why do students who stay on a page get fooled more easily?
o: Misleading sites can look professional and convincing

q.q: Which is a UK fact-checking service?
Which type of content tends to spread fastest online?
What did a major study find about false news on Twitter?
o: It spread faster and further than true news

q.q: What is engagement?
o: Likes, comments, shares and watch time

q.q: Why might an algorithm promote outrageous posts?
Do angry comments count as engagement?
o: Yes, they can boost a post

q.q: What is a bot?
o: An automated account run by software

q.q: How can bot networks spread disinformation?
o: Posting and sharing at huge scale to make it trend

q.q: Why do people believe things that seem popular?
o: We assume many people can't all be wrong

q.q: What is a filter bubble?
o: When an algorithm keeps showing you similar content

q.q: What is an echo chamber?
o: A space where you mostly hear people who agree with you

q.q: How can you burst your filter bubble?
o: Follow a range of reliable sources

q.q: Why are false claims risky inside an echo chamber?
What does the Online Safety Act do?
o: Requires platforms to protect users from illegal and harmful content
q.why: It sets safety duties for platforms.

q.q: Is sharing an intimate deepfake of a real person without consent legal in the UK?
What should you do if a fake image of you is shared?
o: Don't share it, save evidence, report it and tell a trusted adult
Share it to explain it's fake

q.q: What is a fact-checker?
o: A person or organisation that checks claims and publishes what's true

q.q: What are community notes?
o: Users adding context to misleading posts

q.q: What is prebunking?
o: Learning manipulation tricks before you meet them

q.q: Why is prebunking compared to a vaccine?
o: A small, safe dose helps you resist the real thing later

q.q: Which is a manipulation trick?
o: Using a fake expert to sound convincing

q.q: "SHOCKING! They don't want you to know this!" is an example of...
A real photo from 2015 is shared as if from yesterday. This trick is...
A fake account pretends to be your school. This is...
q.why: Pretending to be someone else is impersonation.

q.q: "Either you agree or you hate our town" is an example of...
q.why: It pretends there are only two options.

q.q: What is the best way to correct a friend who shared a fake post?
o: A kind private message with a reliable source
Report your friend to the police
Ignore it and share it too

q.q: Why might correcting someone publicly backfire?
o: They may become defensive and dig in

q.q: Which helps reduce the spread of a false post?
o: Not sharing it and reporting it

q.q: Which of these is a reliable news source for checking claims?
Which is an example of malinformation?
o: Publishing someone's real home address to harass them

q.q: Which helps AI-made images be identified later?
Which is the safest response to a shocking video with no source?
Why do disinformation creators target elections?
Which describes a bot network?
What should you check FIRST about an image that makes you angry?
Why might a deepfake scam call target grandparents?
o: They may trust a familiar voice and act quickly to help
q.why: Trust in a familiar voice is exploited.

q.q: Which family plan helps protect against voice-clone scams?
o: Agree a secret code word for emergencies

q.q: Which of these can be a clue that a video is a deepfake?
o: Lips that don't quite match the words
q.why: Mismatched lips can be a clue.

q.q: A friend says "I saw it on video, so it must be true." What's the best reply?
o: You're right, videos are always real
Videos can be faked now, so check the source

q.q: What does FactCheckNI do?
o: Checks claims made in Northern Ireland

q.q: Which is NOT a SIFT step?
o: Share it to see what people think

q.q: What does it mean when a platform "downranks" a post?
Why is a coordinated group of fake accounts dangerous?
o: It can make a few people look like a crowd

q.q: The best one-word summary of how to respond to shocking content is...
q.why: Pausing gives you time to check.

q.q: A news story quotes an "expert" whose only qualification is "influencer". This is a sign of...
Which helps you trust a photo's origin?
o: Content credentials showing the camera and edit history

q.q: Which statement about AI-detection tools is most accurate?
o: They help, but aren't always right
q.why: Use them as one clue among many.

q.q: Why might a fake news website look professional?
o: Templates make it easy to look trustworthy
Only real sites can look professional

q.q: Which is the best summary of fighting misinformation?
o: Everyone (laws, platforms, fact-checkers and individuals) has a part to play

q.q: What is "clickbait"?
o: A headline designed to make you click, often misleading

q.q: Why do emotional headlines work on us?
o: Strong feelings make us act before thinking

q.q: What might a recommendation algorithm learn if you keep watching angry videos?
o: To show you more of them

q.q: Which is an example of recycling an old photo?
o: A 2010 flood photo shared as last night's storm

q.q: In Northern Ireland, which organisation could you report a crime like a sexual deepfake to?
q.why: The police can help in serious cases.

q.q: Which is a good habit before sharing anything?
o: Ask: who made this, and do trusted sources agree?
Check how many likes it has

q.q: Which is a fully generated deepfake?
o: A video of an event created entirely from a text prompt
q.why: It's created from nothing but a prompt.

q.q: Which reverse image search result would make you most suspicious of a "breaking news" photo?
o: A copy on a news agency site dated today
A copy on the photographer's own site
The same photo appearing years earlier on a different story
q.why: Earlier copies on unrelated stories reveal recycling.

q.q: Which question is part of investigating a source?
o: Who runs this website and what do they gain?
How many images does it have?

q.q: Which is an example of a platform slowing the spread of false content?
o: Turning off comments for everyone everywhere
Adding a warning label and showing it to fewer people

q.q: Why do false stories often seem more interesting than true ones?
o: They can be invented to be surprising and new
